name: Core stability (plank, dead bug)

lead: Core stability training uses holds like the plank and controlled movements like the dead bug to train the trunk. Posture communities include it in pelvic tilt routines for more upright posture and a tighter-looking midsection.

The exercises train the abdominal, back and hip muscles to hold the spine and pelvis in position under load or movement. Encyclopedic sources say research support for the core stability model is limited and that core-specific training performs about as well as general exercise at best; nothing found tests it for appearance.

paras: People do planks, side planks and dead bugs as short sets a few times a week, usually alongside stretching and glute work in posture programs.
Generally low risk. Back pain during exercise is usually referred to a clinician.

angle.text: Planks and dead bugs are used for posture and pelvic tilt and to firm the midsection by training the muscles that hold the trunk in position. Core-stability research shows modest benefit over general exercise; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Core stability is a person's ability to control the position and movement of the trunk, meaning the muscles around the spine, pelvis and abdomen. [1] The plank, an isometric hold resembling a push-up position, and the dead bug, a lying limb-movement drill, are two of the most common exercises used to train it. [1][2] People in posture and looksmaxxing communities use them to build a stronger trunk, with the aim of standing taller and more upright, correcting anterior pelvic tilt and showing a firmer, leaner-looking midsection. [3]

Sports-medicine reviews describe the core as the group of trunk muscles surrounding the spine and abdominal viscera, working together with gluteal, hip and paraspinal muscles to stabilise the spine and pelvis. [4] Core strengthening is used in sport and as a therapeutic exercise for low back pain. [4][5] Wikipedia lists planks, side planks and dead bugs among exercises suggested for anterior pelvic tilt, while noting that the sourcing for that section is weak. [3]

Research on the core stability model is mixed. A 2010 critical review re-examined its original findings and principles, [6] and Wikipedia states that core-specific training has not been shown to beat general exercise for injury prevention or performance. [1] A 2023 meta-analysis found core training was examined across balance, throwing and jumping outcomes in healthy people. [7] No study found has tested plank or dead bug training for pelvic tilt or visual appearance.

paras: The core muscles listed in encyclopedic sources include the pelvic floor, transversus abdominis, multifidus, internal and external obliques, rectus abdominis, erector spinae and diaphragm. Breathing can influence core posture and movement. [1]

The plank is also called a front hold or abdominal bridge. A forearm plank rests the body on the forearms and toes; variants include the side plank, reverse plank and extended plank. Primary muscles for the front plank are given as the erector spinae, rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis, with the shoulder girdle, glutes and legs as secondary. The side plank emphasises the obliques, transversus abdominis and hip abductors. [2]
The dead bug is performed lying on the back, moving opposite arm and leg while keeping the lower back controlled.

Planks, side planks and dead bugs appear in posture programs alongside glute bridges and hip thrusts as anterior pelvic tilt measures. [3] Proponents link a stronger trunk with better posture and a leaner-looking midsection.

On T Nation, one lifter's suggested quick routine for trunk work lists kettlebell plank transfers, dead bugs and weighted back extensions, framed around back and lifting health rather than appearance. [8]

A review in Current Sports Medicine Reports summarises the anatomy of the core, how core strengthening is progressed, and the evidence for its efficacy in musculoskeletal conditions. [4] Another review discusses the role of core stability in athletic function. [9] A critical 2010 review argues that the principles of spinal stabilisation approaches should be re-examined against wider knowledge of motor control. [6]

Wikipedia reports that trunk-specific exercise has not been shown to prevent sports injuries or improve sports performance. [1] A review of 270 trials in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, cited by Wikipedia, found isometric exercises including planks and wall sits were more effective than other exercise types for lowering blood pressure. [2] That finding concerns blood pressure, not posture or appearance.

No studies found testing plank or dead bug training for pelvic tilt or appearance. Studies of core stability training more broadly include a meta-analysis comparing core stability exercise with general exercise for chronic low back pain, [5] a 2023 meta-analysis of core training and athletic performance in healthy people, [7] a review of core stability in non-specific chronic low back pain, [10] and a trial in people with non-specific low back pain. [11]
